S000033.text: WE NEED A NEW FOREIGN POLICY. Amidst the fiasco of the war in Iran, Americans need to rethink the very foundations of our foreign policy and how we go forward in a very different direction — a direction which focuses on peace, democracy and economic and social justice. Let us not forget: The war in Vietnam was based on a lie. In that war over 58,000 Americans died, hundreds of thousands were wounded and millions of Vietnamese civilians lost their lives. The war in Iraq was based on a lie. In that war 4,492 Americans died, tens of thousands were wounded and hundreds of thousands Iraqi civilians lost their lives. The current war in Iran was based on a lie. In this war 14 Americans have been killed, hundreds have been wounded and up to ten thousand civilians in the region have lost their lives. Meanwhile, with 60% of our people living paycheck to paycheck, we have a military budget of over one trillion dollars — much of it going to the extremely profitable military-industrial complex. In terms of the Middle East, here are our major allies: Israel: a nation, now controlled by right-wing extremists, which has committed genocide in Gaza, plotted with Trump to start the illegal and unconstitutional war in Iran, and is now actively obstructing a meaningful pathway towards peace as it continues to attack Lebanon’s civilian population. Saudi Arabia: a nation controlled by the wealthiest family in the world who run a dictatorship that treats women as third-class citizens and tolerates no opposition or dissent. According to U.S. intelligence, the Saudi leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, had American journalist Jamal Khashoggi murdered in its Istanbul consulate because of his criticism of the regime. UAE: a nation which is an authoritarian monarchy with no free press, no free elections and no independent civil society — built on the labor of migrant workers who make up 80% of its population. Beyond its borders, the UAE has armed the Rapid Support Forces — a paramilitary group the United States government has formally determined is committing genocide in Sudan. Qatar: a nation which is also an authoritarian monarchy controlled by the Al Thani family, one of the most powerful and wealthy royal families in the world. Unbelievably, 91% of Qatar’s population is migrant labor who are ruthlessly oppressed. While building World Cup stadiums in Qatar, thousands of workers died as a result of horrendous working conditions. The politics of the Middle East are complicated, and no one believes that we can bring peace, prosperity and democracy to the region tomorrow. But clearly, we need a very different approach than what we have right now. We need a foreign policy that actually reflects our values and which must start with a simple premise: the United States will not provide weapons and diplomatic cover to governments — whether in Tel Aviv, Riyadh, Abu Dhabi or Doha — that engage in systematic human rights violations. And it means, at long last, building a foreign policy centered around human rights, respect for international law and multilateralism — and one that holds war criminals accountable no matter whom they may be.

Yesterday, the House Appropriations Committee debated the Fiscal Year 2027 bill that funds the U.S. Dept. of Homeland Security. Unfortunately, this bill does not include commonsense guardrails, that most Americans want, to ensure that peoples' civil liberties are protected. But this bill guts the department's Offices of Civil Rights and Civil Liberties Office and the Inspector General which helps prevent fraud, waste, and abuse - something Democrats and Republicans want! While I supported an effort to restore their funding, along with other amendments, we could not improve the bill. As the U.S. House and Senate continues work on the bill, I hope we find a bipartisan pathway forward that protects our country and its people, including the most fundamental rights enshrined in our Constitution. In addition to my remarks in support of restoring funding for these offices, you can watch my opening remarks in committee: https://youtu.be/kJyZjGDJAMY

On Tuesday, the House Appropriations Committee debated funding that affects every American, but the bill on which we ended up voting would make healthcare more expensive as well as education and job training less accessible. For example, the bill guts funding to Job Corps and I know from first-hand experience how important this program is to local economies. The Turner Job Corps Center in Albany is just one of over 120 centers located in every state in America, in Democratic- and Republican-represented districts. Not only do these centers help train people to achieve gainful employment, but their training is also tailored towards workforce development that local businesses need. It is a win-win situation. As co-chair of the bipartisan Congressional Job Corps Caucus that I lead with Rep. Guthrie, a Republican from Kentucky, I spoke in favor of an amendment, offered by a Republican colleague of mine from Montana, and I know a majority of my colleagues on the committee would have supported the amendment but it was withdrawn. Because we could not improve the bill on this and other fronts during the debate, I had to vote against it. I am hopeful that as the appropriations process continues, we build a better bill that meets the needs of Georgia and hardworking Americans across our country. You can watch my remarks about the full bill here: https://youtu.be/oBHft1eKv2I

C001053.text: Terrorists. Cartels. Human traffickers. Drug smugglers. Each day, ICE and Border Patrol agents and officers confront these threats head-on to keep America safe. It’s exactly why I have consistently voted to comprehensively resource these law enforcement professionals as they carry out their security missions. While the far-left hoped to eradicate funding for critical operations and weaken our border security apparatus, House Republicans have made clear that we will continue to support those who defend our homeland and keep our communities safe. That's why we passed the Secure America Act today. However, while I do not regret the objective of our actions today, I am appalled by the complete failure of Senate Democrats that led us to this moment. Chuck Schumer and his radical caucus twice shut down the government, instigating chaos across the nation. Since then, they have continued to diminish Article I and forced the use of reconciliation. It’s wrong – and deliberately undermines the appropriations process. The Constitution entrusts Congress with the power of the purse. Yet, in great irony, the Senate has shown greater concern for protecting an internal rule than fulfilling its constitutional duty. The filibuster is nothing more than an institutional habit. It is neither mentioned nor sanctioned in our founding documents. I would remind my peers on the other side of the Rotunda that no chamber precedent is greater than the bedrock of our Republic. Members swear an oath to uphold the Constitution – not the filibuster. I thoroughly regret the erosion of Article I authority that Senate Democrats have instigated, and the price everyday Americans have been forced to pay as a result. I hope the months-long charade that led us to this moment serves as a reminder that no partisan fixation is worth shutting down the government, abandoning constitutional responsibilities, and forcing Congress into extraordinary measures simply to perform its most basic duties. I believe in the Constitution, the power of the purse, and completing the appropriations process. I also believe in keeping the homeland safe. The Senate may have abandoned proper governing, but I will not abandon those who stand watch over our borders and protect our communities. Our work, of course, doesn’t end here. As the Fiscal Year 2027 Appropriations markups near completion, I am reminded that governing is a choice. The work I do, the votes I cast, and the actions I take will always be guided by one principle: fulfilling our obligations to the American people

For 39 years, Governor Bill Anoatubby has led my tribe, the Chickasaw Nation, with remarkable vision, a strategic hand, and unwavering dedication. His leadership has transformed not only the trajectory of the Nation, but the lives of the Chickasaw people.   Economically, his tenure has been nothing short of historic and unprecedented. Through Governor Anoatubby’s steady leadership, the Chickasaw Nation did more than just achieve its goals of economic development and self-sufficiency – it surpassed them. Under his guidance, the tribe evolved from dependence on federal funding to one that is self-sufficient and prosperous on its own. Today, thanks to him, the Chickasaw Nation supports more than 22,000 jobs and contributes $3.7 billion annually to Oklahoma’s economy, including $1.2 billion in wages and benefits.   However, Governor Anoatubby’s impact cannot be measured by just economics. Throughout his lengthy tenure, he also placed a significant emphasis on preserving and sharing the precious heritage of the Chickasaw Nation. Through initiatives such as the Chickasaw Nation Division of Arts and Humanities and the Chickasaw Cultural Center, he ensured that our history, language, arts, and culture would continue to inspire future generations.   These achievements, on top of many others, make it unmistakably clear: Governor Bill Anoatubby is the most consequential Chickasaw Nation leader since the removal period. And his influence has extended past just the Chickasaw Nation. His leadership and impact are respected by every Oklahoman.   For nearly four decades, Governor Anoatubby has embodied true commitment to the Chickasaw people and Oklahoma. The powerful combination of his leadership, vision, and generosity has allowed all of us in our state to shape a brighter future for ourselves and all those touched by the results of his leadership. On a personal level, I am fortunate to call Governor Anoatubby a mentor and a trusted friend.   His retirement is an enormous loss for the Chickasaw Nation, all Indian Country, and the state of Oklahoma. However, he leaves the tribe stronger than he found it, as he hands it off to his very competent and bright son, Chris, the Lieutenant Governor. I have no doubt Chris will carry on his father’s legacy with wisdom, competence, and care, and I look forward to seeing everything the future holds for the Chickasaw Nation.   In conclusion, to Governor Anoatubby, congratulations on a truly remarkable career and a lifetime of service. Thank you for your leadership, your vision, your friendship, and the legacy you leave behind. I wish you, Janice, and your entire family the best as you enter this next chapter.

That's why I've been pushing for increased sterile fly production, stronger USDA resources, and additional support for ranchers and producers. I urged the USDA to establish a domestic sterile fly production facility, supported efforts to provide $300 million for domestic sterile fly production capacity, and secured House Appropriations Committee language directing APHIS to make a domestic facility a priority. Yesterday, I joined Commissioner Chad McIntosh, State Representative Richard Raymond, Mayor Dr. Victor Treviño, local leaders, and partners for the signing ceremony marking a major milestone in the proposed expansion of the World Trade Bridge. With the U.S. International Boundary and Water Commission’s approval of the binational joint review, the project can now move forward toward expanding capacity at one of the nation’s busiest trade crossings. The expansion will help reduce congestion, improve commercial traffic flow, and strengthen the supply chains that support jobs and economic growth across South Texas and the country. As a senior member of the House Appropriations Committee, I’ll continue working with our local, state, and federal partners to help move this project forward and ensure Laredo remains a leader in international trade. This is an important step forward for Laredo, South Texas, and the future of U.S.-Mexico trade.

During the American Revolutionary War, General George Washington and the Continental Army endured a difficult winter encampment at Valley Forge in the winter of 1777–1778. What began as a collection of regular troops and colonial militias emerged under Washington's leadership as a disciplined and unified fighting force committed to the cause of liberty and independence. On June 19, 1778, the Continental Army marched out of Valley Forge and headed toward Monmouth Courthouse in New Jersey to stand against the British Army. Valley Forge remains a powerful reminder of the perseverance, and leadership that helped shape our nation.

These communities already faced some of the highest energy costs in the country, but those prices have now risen even further—often to $10 a gallon or more—and have been locked in for months, sometimes longer, because they only receive fuel shipments once or twice a year when sea ice has receded. Congress can complement the state's efforts and ensure that those who face the toughest burdens from higher energy costs in Alaska and around the nation have the support they need to make it through this difficult time.

Today we honor the life and legacy of Gilbert “Butch” Wallace, a devoted husband, father, grandfather, friend, and public servant whose impact on our community will be felt for generations. Butch is survived by his beloved wife of 48 years, Carolyn Wallace, their two daughters, Heather Wallace and Michelle Boone, and grandson Tyler Muller. Together they built a family grounded in faith, service, and love. The Wilson family always welcomed him as “Uncle Butch,” Attorney General Alan Wilson and Palmetto State Armory founder Julian Wilson were especially encouraged by “Uncle Butch.” A Florida native, Butch attended Florida State University where he earned a degree in Communications and Business. He went on to build a successful State Farm Agency, serving his community for 48 years. Through his work, he not only helped countless families and businesses, butalso, created jobs and contributed to the economic growth of our state. For more than 20 years, Butch has served as avalued member of my staff, where he touched the lives of countless South Carolinians, including my own. His wisdom and unwavering commitment to others made him an indispensable member of Team Wilson and a trusted friend of all those who worked alongside him. His dedication to service extended far beyond his professional life. He was deeply involved in his community serving as a Charter Member and President of the West Metro Rotary Club, President of the National Kidney Foundation of South Carolina, a member of the National Federation of Independent Business State Advisory Council, and a member of the Boy Scouts of America Indian Waters Council Board.   Additionally, in 2019, he was a recipient of the Order of the Palmetto, South Carolina’s highest civilian award. His commitment to civic engagement led him to serve in many political leadership roles including as Chairman of the Lexington County Republican Party and as a delegate to many state and county conventions. Butch lived a life defined by service, integrity, and kindness. South Carolina is better because of his contributions, and all who knew him are better for having called him a friend. He leaves behind a legacy of leadership, compassion, and service that will endure long beyond his lifetime. May we honor Butch by striving to serve others with the same dedication and grace that he demonstrated throughout his remarkable life.

F000466.text: This morning at Historic Boone Farm in Middletown Township, on Juneteenth, our community witnessed something truly special: a dream realized. The African American Museum of Bucks County now has a home worthy of the history it preserves, the stories it carries, and the generations it will teach. On a day that reminds us freedom must be taught, protected, and remembered, this museum gives our community a permanent place to do that sacred work. This day belongs to my dear friend, the late Linda Salley. For years, Linda carried these stories across our community—into schools, churches, libraries, and gathering places—because she knew Bucks County’s African American history deserved to be known, honored, and passed on. She was right. Working alongside Linda and the AAMBC team to bring this vision to life has been one of the great honors of my service, including securing $2 million to help complete the restoration and expansion of Boone Farm. Linda and I shared a deep belief that this history deserved more than a temporary home. It deserved permanence. It deserved a place to stand. And today, because of her vision and the dedication of so many, it has one. The story of Bucks County cannot be fully told without the stories this museum preserves. And because of Linda’s faith, leadership, and love for this community, those stories will continue to teach, inspire, and endure for generations. Congratulations to the entire AAMBC team, board, staff, volunteers, partners, and every person who made this possible—and my sincere thanks to my incredible friend, Pastor Don Schuler, for providing such special remarks on my behalf.

On June 19, 1865, more than two years after the Emancipation Proclamation, Union troops arrived in Galveston, Texas, to announce and enforce emancipation—a turning point in our nation’s long march toward justice. For those who had been denied the truth of their freedom, Juneteenth marked a long-overdue day of liberation. For our nation, it remains a defining moment in America’s ongoing journey toward justice, equality, and human dignity. That is why, in 2021, I helped lead the effort to establish Juneteenth as a federal holiday—to honor this historic moment, preserve its rightful place in our national memory, and recognize the generations of Americans whose courage, faith, perseverance, and sacrifice have carried our country closer to its founding ideals. As Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. reminded us, “Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.” Today, we honor this legacy by reflecting on that truth and renewing our commitment to justice, equality, freedom, and dignity for all.

Join me in congratulating Aiden Ertwine of Warrington, Magnus Figueroa of Holicong, Kian Wilson of Pipersville, and Mitav Mehta of Furlong, all of Troop 71, on earning the rank of Eagle Scout! Each of these young men completed a meaningful service project rooted in stewardship, conservation, and care for the natural world around us. For his project, Mitav built an 85-foot boardwalk at Heritage Conservancy’s Jackson Pond Nature Preserve, helping protect sensitive habitats by reducing erosion from runoff while providing visitors with a safe, elevated pathway to experience the preserve. Magnus also partnered with Heritage Conservancy, creating an informational kiosk for one of its preserved properties and replacing a drainage pipe to help improve the site for future visitors. At Aark Wildlife Rehabilitation and Education Center, Aiden created a mammal enclosure for rabies-vector mammals in need of rehabilitation, while Kian built a new enclosure to provide mammals and rodents with a safe sanctuary as they recover and receive care. Together, these projects reflect the very best of Scouting: seeing a need, stepping forward, and using leadership and hard work to strengthen the places, organizations, and natural resources that make our community so special. Congratulations to each of you—and thank you to your families, Scout leaders, Troop 71, and the entire PA-1 Scouting community for continuing to lead through service.

Juneteenth is a celebration of freedom, but it is also a reminder that freedom was never fully given – it’s a continual battle. More than 160 years later, Black Americans are still fighting for justice, representation, and the right to have our voices heard. At a time when Black political power is under attack and voting rights are being rolled back, we cannot treat this moment as just history. The disgraceful Louisiana v. Callais' decision is part of a broader effort to turn back the clock on decades of progress and weaken fair representation across the country. This Juneteenth, we recommit ourselves to the unfinished works of freedom: protecting voting rights, defending democracy, closing the racial wealth gap, and building a country where every community has power, opportunity, and a voice. The march toward a more perfect union continues. #Juneteenth #NV04

In Las Vegas, I was honored to convene a roundtable with my mentor, @repjamesclyburn, and Nevada faith and civil rights leaders to listen directly to the voices trusted by our communities.    At a time when voting rights, civil rights, health care, education, and economic opportunity are under attack, these conversations matter. The people closest to the pain must be closest to the power.    Nevada has always been shaped by leaders who organize, advocate, and fight for the dignity of every family. I will take what was shared in this room back to Washington, because our communities' voices belong in the halls of Congress.    We are not backing down. We are staying organized, united, and ready to fight for the future our families deserve.

But what I saw here is something everyone should see: lessons about the injustices of our past, which help us appreciate the progress we have made and remind us exactly why freedom is still worth fighting for.    This Administration can try to replace exhibits like this, but it cannot replace history – not the shameful parts we learn from, nor the freedoms we celebrate. From day one, the majority of Americans did not want this war. If President Trump had come to Congress, as the Constitution requires, we would have told him that. But this Administration pressed on anyway – despite the cost, despite the law, and despite the will of the people. Now, after billions of taxpayer dollars spent and 13 American servicemembers’ lives lost, we are no better off in Iran than we were before the war began. Iran’s nuclear ambitions have not been eliminated. Iran has more control over the Strait of Hormuz now than it did before this war, and more access to capital than before the war as well. Here at home, we have paid more at the gas pump and on other essentials as a result. We would be in the same position, if not better, had President Trump never torn up the JCPOA, President Obama’s 2015 nuclear agreement with Iran. This is what happens when you disregard the will of the people, ignore the work and lessons of those before you, and start a war before understanding and defining your objectives or strategy. This is what happens with President Trump and Secretary Hegseth at the helm. We cannot afford more of this irresponsible leadership.

Trump never should have gotten us into this deranged war. He never should have torn up President Obama’s Iran deal. While I’m grateful that the fighting may cease and our troops will no longer suffer from Trump and Hegseth’s incompetence, it’s clear that Trump was more worried about his poll numbers than protecting American interests.

Yesterday, before watching the world’s best golfers compete at the U.S. Open at Shinnecock Hills, Kaylie, Reagan, and I spent time with my friends from the Shinnecock Nation on their tribal land. Their story is one of faith, family, resilience, and perseverance, a story I grow to appreciate more with every visit. Vice Chairman Lance Gumbs gave us a personal tour of the Shinnecock Museum, the reservation, and the resting places of some of the Nation’s ancestors. As we focused on the headstones, I was struck by how many Shinnecocks had served in the U.S. military. Lance shared that Native Americans have long served at higher rates than the general population, a tradition that continues today. In fact, since 9/11, roughly 19% of Native Americans have served in the Armed Forces, compared to about 14% of Americans from other ethnic groups, a remarkable testament to their patriotism and commitment to service. After the tour, I met with Chairwoman Lisa Goree and the Council of Trustees at the Nation’s headquarters in Southampton. We talked about the nation’s 800 people, and what the council is doing to promote education, economic independence, and quality of life. For more than 13,000 years, the Shinnecock people have called this land home. As skilled whalers, artisans, and steadfast stewards of a rich Algonquian heritage, they have helped shape the history and character of the East End. Their enduring contributions, strength, and spirit are an important part of what makes hosting the 2026 U.S. Open at Shinnecock Hills so meaningful.

J000311.text: On this day in 1944, over 34,000 American soldiers crowded together in small, amphibious boats en route to Omaha Beach. As the boats landed on the beach, and their bow ramps dropped down leading the men ashore, unrelenting machine gun fire rained down from enemy bunkers. Undeterred, the American and Allied forces emerged from the battle victorious, but not without a heavy cost. Over 2,500 Americans died at Omaha Beach. One of them was 1st Lieutenant Thomas Royce Dallas Jr. from our Congressional District in Griffin, Georgia, who drew his last breath on the shores of Omaha Beach. As we remember the heroism Americans exhibited on D-Day and we reflect on the cost of freedom, may we remember and be inspired by the names and faces of those brave soldiers who died in service to our Country.

Today, we fully reopened the Tyrone Post Office! Before I was sworn into Congress, I promised to reopen the Tyrone Post Office, which had previously suffered extensive structural damage due to a fire.  As of today, the Tyrone Post Office is fully open for business. During a Congressional oversight hearing, I asked the Postmaster General to accelerate the Post Office’s reconstruction, which had been delayed for years.  He and his team swiftly reacted, and worked closely with my team to achieve this goal. Thank you to Tyrone Mayor Eric Dial and the Tyrone Town Council for your partnership and forceful advocacy, and thank you to Postmaster General David Steiner, and Kayla Dufrene, Brandy Jackson, and Sharon Alston of the Postal Service for your leadership on this important project.

Donald Trump initiated a war with Iran without the support of Congress and the American people. His actions used up billions of dollars in weaponry, resulted in billions of dollars of damage to American military installations, billions in additional costs for consumers, and most tragically, cost the lives of 13 US service members. Now, after 5 months of seeking a way out of the mess he created, President Trump presents us with a “deal,” which grants Iran access to a $300 billion reconstruction fund, provides immediate sanctions relief for the IRGC and its terrorist proxies, and does nothing to quell Iran's nuclear ambitions. It may also result in Iran imposing a maritime fee on oil transported through the Straits of Hormuz, an international waterway, putting a higher price tag on oil passed off on consumers. Worst of all, Iran’s ballistic missile and drone programs remain untouched, leaving America and our allies as exposed as ever to the Iranian regime. I see no art in this deal. President Trump has clearly missed the mark in achieving a result that benefits the American people. This agreement must be fully vetted by Congress with all relevant officials involved facing tough questioning; they must make the case for why they think this deal is merited. It is, on the surface, a very poor result.

WORLD_INDIA_PM.text: સંઘ પ્રદેશ દાદરા અને નગર હવેલી અને દમણ અને દીવના પ્રશાસક શ્રી પ્રફુલભાઈ પટેલના ધર્મપત્ની શ્રીમતી ભાવનાબેન પટેલના અવસાનના સમાચારથી દુઃખ થયું. વર્ષોથી આ પરિવાર સાથે મારો નિકટનો પરિચય અને ઘનિષ્ઠ સંબંધ રહ્યો છે. આ દુઃખની ઘડીમાં હું પરિવારજનોને હૃદયપૂર્વક સાંત્વના પાઠવું છું અને પરમાત્મા સ્વર્ગસ્થ આત્માને શાંતિ આપે તેવી પ્રાર્થના કરું છું. ૐ શાંતિ….!!!
